#9565. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

#9564. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9562. For A Juicier Burger, Make It Scottish-Style

Even if you have the perfect blend of meats, some burger patties can stand a little extra moisture to keep them juicy after exposure to high heat. While it may be a less conventional choice, black pudding has a remarkable capacity to make burgers juicier, and the method is actually quite similar to other juicy ground meat recipes.

Black pudding is a type of blood sausage consisting of a congealed blend of oats, spices, animal blood, and sometimes assorted organ meats. The use of oats is quite similar to using milk-soaked breadcrumbs in meatballs to keep them moist. When you introduce a bit of black pudding into burgers, the oats can help retain moisture within the patties, keeping them juicy. This helps maintain a consistent level of moisture without adding excess liquid that could inhibit a good crust.

While you can always use breadcrumbs or other conventional ingredients instead, black pudding is far meatier and more similar to a patty's flavor profile. Rich in umami and seasonings of its own, it adds so much more than just juiciness. Black pudding can also crisp up on a grill, griddle, or in a pan, so you won't be sacrificing texture for the sake of moisture. Using roughly one part black pudding to two parts meat ensures you can taste both and get a proper level of juiciness, even when using lean blends.

Black pudding is something you may rarely encounter in the U.S., and regional varieties can make it difficult to find the perfect one for burger patties. While just about any type can get the job done, texture and flavor profile are important considerations, and you'll have to mix it in properly for the best results.

Black pudding isn't monolithic and ranges from the crisped discs served in a full English breakfast to boudin noir in France. The crumbly texture of Scottish black pudding is ideal and makes it easier to add to a burger blend, whether that's beef or another meat mixture. When ingredients are easy to incorporate, it prevents you from overworking the meat and helps you grill burgers like a pro, achieving a tender result that doesn't firm up into a sausage puck. Scottish varieties also make ample use of oatmeal as a binder, so you're more likely to get that juiciness you want.

Scottish black puddings also tend to keep the seasonings quite simple, creating something delicious but not overly complex. By focusing on a simple blend of salt, pepper, and aromatics, they leave you more room to season your burgers to your liking. While boudin noir is delicious thanks to its blend of spices like nutmeg, these can easily clash with what's in your seasoning cabinet and make pairings difficult. Simple seasonings also let you add more to your blend, so you don't have to worry so much about ratios.

#9560. REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?

You use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built. Maybe it is a fast search bar, a clever clipboard trick, or a mechanic in an old game. Until recently, finding out meant months of learning disassemblers and reading assembly code. A new open-source project called REA changes that. It has earned more than 430,000 stars on GitHub, and in this guide I will explain what it does, which problems it solves, and how you can start using it today.

Reverse engineering is the practice of studying finished software to understand how it works. It is powerful, but it has never been beginner-friendly. If you have tried it, or even thought about trying it, you have probably run into these obstacles.

Reading assembly code and pseudocode takes a long time to learn. Many curious developers give up before they get their first useful result.

An Electron app needs one approach. An Android APK needs another. A .NET assembly, a native binary, and a website each have their own tools, file formats, and tricks.

Even experts can spend hours following one function through strings, calls, and references just to understand a single small feature.

If you ask a general chatbot how an app works, it may give a confident answer that is simply invented. Without evidence, you cannot tell what is real.

Connecting analysis tools to an AI agent usually requires custom scripts and configuration, and it is easy to break.

REA is a free, MIT-licensed project that connects your AI agent to professional reverse engineering tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use external tools. In simple terms, REA acts as a bridge between your agent and the software you want to understand. Here is how it answers each problem above.

You do not need the app’s source code. You point your agent at the app, ask a question, and REA helps it trace the answer.

The same workflows are available from the terminal, so you can also script them without an agent. Analysis runs locally on your machine. Your agent receives the tool results, and your AI provider’s own data policy applies to that part.

The range of supported targets is one of REA’s biggest strengths. These are the main groups.

REA returns pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls, and references. Deep native analysis uses an engine you already have, such as Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or Kuna. It also supports GNU objdump and Rizin for offline inspection.

This is the easiest place to start, because static JavaScript analysis needs no native engine. REA recovers modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC connections, and native add-on relationships.

REA can inspect APK manifests, classes, decompiled methods, signatures, and resources. Through adb, it can also look at packages, processes, and logs on an emulator or a real phone. Flutter apps and JEB projects are supported too.

For .NET assemblies, REA reads metadata, CIL instructions, and native dependencies without running the program.

REA can inspect page structure, scripts, and network activity using a Chrome-family browser. It can also read saved HAR and Fiddler SAZ files to examine requests, responses, and exposed payloads.

The list continues with Go and Rust binaries, GPU code objects, GGUF and safetensors model files, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK archives, PE imports and certificates, ELF notes, Linux kernel modules, WebAssembly, EVM bytecode, SQLite databases, firmware images, packet captures, and PyInstaller executables. Most of these use built-in static inspection, so no extra software is required.

The project publishes several case studies on its website.

REA can record a web app session and turn its API calls into tools an AI agent can use. It then exports a runnable environment for reinforcement learning or for testing how well an agent completes tasks. With a saved HAR file, the command looks like this:

You then run the result with AgentEnv and Docker, and add your own tasks and reward checks.

You need Node.js and npm. The project lists supported Node versions as 22.x (22.23.4 or newer), 24.x (24.22.1 or newer), or 26.12.1 and above.

Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents. It shows you the proposed changes first and keeps backups of your existing configuration.

The new MCP server is loaded when the agent starts again.

You can inspect an extracted Electron app or ASAR file directly:

To keep REA installed, run npm install --global rea-agents. REA changes quickly, so use rea update to stay current. Updating is also the first fix to try if you run into a bug.

REA combines the reach of dozens of analysis tools with the convenience of an AI agent. It helps you understand software you do not have source code for, and it backs each conclusion with evidence instead of guesses. The range of supported formats, from native binaries to Electron apps to Android devices, is unusually broad for a free tool.

Developers, security researchers, students, software preservationists, and anyone who wants to understand how an app works.

Use REA only on software you own or are authorized to examine.

The project is intended for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you have permission to study. It does not permit cracked tools, stolen license keys, or bypassing license restrictions. Read the project’s disclaimer before you start.

Also be careful where you download it from. The project warns that a similar repository name or a copied README does not make a download official. Use only these sources:

Only for deep native binary analysis. JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native engine, and setup can install Hopper with your approval.

No. Analysis runs locally. Your agent sees the results, and its provider has its own data policy.

Any agent that supports local MCP servers can use it.

Update first, because a recent release may already include the fix. If the problem continues, open an issue on GitHub with your REA version, the target type, the steps to reproduce, and the error output.

The old problem was simple: understanding software without source code took too much skill, too many tools, and too much time. REA’s answer is just as simple. It gives your AI agent the tools to investigate, and it requires the agent to show its evidence. Whether you want to learn how a favorite feature works, study a classic game, or inspect an Electron app, REA is a strong place to start. Just make sure you use it only on software you are allowed to examine.

#9558. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9555. Add This Creamy Ingredient To Tuna Salad For A Major Flavor Boost (Hint: It's Not Mayo Or Yogurt)

Whether you like to enjoy it between a couple of slices of bread, spread it on crackers, or eat it on its own with a spoon, tuna salad is an easy dish to prepare that makes use of kitchen staples. Despite its popularity and the many ways you can take tuna salad to the next level, though, many recipes include the same condiment to give it richness: mayonnaise. Sure, there are different brands that each have their own unique characteristics — but what do you do when you want to switch things up without losing out on the creamy mouthfeel? Try using crème fraîche.

This rich product originated in France, and its name literally translates to "fresh cream" in English, though don't let its name fool you. It's actually a fermented dairy product made from cream, which makes it similar to but different from sour cream. For starters, it has a higher fat content, giving it a deliciously luscious consistency that complements the texture of the tuna well. It's also less acidic than sour cream, whose tanginess might not play well with every type of ingredient you want to add to your recipe. Furthermore, crème fraîche typically doesn't have added thickeners or stabilizers, which some consumers may want to avoid. It also has its own unique flavor that's slightly nutty and just a little sweet.

Nevertheless, it can be pricier than sour cream, with an 8-ounce container of the former sometimes costing as much as twice the price of a 16-ounce container of the latter. However, you can transform sour cream into crème fraîche at home with some heavy cream.

The first question you may have about using crème fraîche in tuna salad is how much you should use. If you're using one 5-ounce can of fish, add about a quarter cup of the rich, cultured cream to begin with, give it a stir, and add more if you prefer a creamier salad. Because crème fraîche has a high fat content, you'll want to use tuna packed in water rather than oil to prevent your finished dish from becoming too greasy.

Beyond salt and pepper, there are several additions that will take the finished dish to the next level. Grainy mustard can offset the richness of the crème fraîche, along with some capers and finely chopped shallots. For a kick, you can also add a small amount of prepared horseradish or a few dashes of hot sauce. Chopped fresh parsley will impart freshness, and a squeeze of lemon juice can easily brighten the whole preparation.

Crème fraîche isn't the only thing that will give your tuna salad a creamy mouthfeel and rich flavor, though. If you like a little extra tanginess and want to save money, sour cream may be a perfect base for an Eastern European-inspired tuna salad with dill and chopped pickles. You can also use Mexican-style crema, which is a little milder than sour cream but tangier than crème fraîche and pairs beautifully with chopped jalapeños. If you want something significantly milder, though, mascarpone is an excellent option and lets you get really creative with your seasonings and add-ins, as it won't compete with any of the elements of your recipe.

#9553. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

#9552. 9 Ranch Dressing Brands With High-Quality Ingredients

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Ranch is one of the most popular salad dressings and dips in the country. But many of the tangy products are made with less-than-ideal ingredients. That's why we've created this list of organic and clean-ingredient ranch brands. Not only do dressings with high-quality ingredients generally taste better due to the lack of fillers, but they're healthier, too. That's thanks to the products being made without artificial ingredients or synthetic preservatives. The fact that you can use less and still get a lot of flavor makes these an economical choice, as well.

Because these brands use minimal stabilizers and preservatives, it's important to know they won't last as long as other shelf-stable ranch dressings. Usually, a bottle of ranch can stay safe for up to three months after opening, but with these companies' products often using real dairy, it's best to treat them more like homemade. That means it's safest to consume these dressings within one month of opening, although some can last up to two months. But with all the different ways you can use ranch, leftovers shouldn't be a problem.

Primal Kitchen was founded in 2015 as a way to bring clean-ingredient condiments to the public. Today, it sells over 80 products, such as organic unsweetened ketchup, steak sauce, and mayonnaise made with avocado oil. The company uses plant-based oils and other high-quality ingredients in its ranch, which has no added sugars or conventional stabilizers. Primal Kitchen Ranch, which can be found in many grocery stores, is also made with cage-free eggs, is certified Keto-safe and gluten-free, and is Whole30 approved.

This product is dairy-free, relying on a mix of organic apple cider vinegar, spices, herbs, and egg yolks to create the rich, tangy taste of ranch. Mushroom extract takes the place of synthetic preservatives to keep the dressing fresh, and the dip's base is made from avocado oil-based mayo. In fact, many of Primal Kitchen's dressings and sauces contain avocado oil because it's a sustainable source of monounsaturated fats that are linked to lowering "bad" LDL cholesterol and reducing blood pressure.

Reviewers have reported the sauce having a distinctly herby taste, with pronounced dill that wasn't overwhelming. The dressing is great as is, but feel free to add a bit of lime to turn the ranch into the base for incredible nachos. Or if you want an unexpectedly delicious flavor, add some edible lavender to the dip. The aromatic flower complements the heavier sauce and makes this a wonderful addition to a chopped veggies board.

Ohio-based slaw and salad dressing company Marzetti was founded way back in 1896. Today, it's respected enough by customers to have ranked No. 32 in the Food and Beverage section on Newsweek's list of the Most Trustworthy Companies in America in 2026. So it's probably not surprising to learn that Marzetti has earned not just one, but two spots on this list.

This first one is for the Classic Ranch Dressing. This product is made without artificial flavors, preservatives, or high fructose corn syrup. It also uses actual buttermilk instead of powder, giving it an authentic tangy taste and a creamy consistency. The brand sells it in a refrigerated 13-ounce option or as a 22-ounce shelf-stable bottle. Fans of the classic ranch have praised the product's taste and versatility, alongside the fact that the larger version comes in a squeeze bottle, allowing them to easily portion out exactly how much they'd like.

Created by a woman who wanted to ensure the dressing she was using was healthy, Tessemae's makes its products without artificial ingredients, and every ranch in its line of six is Whole30-approved and made without any elements harvested from genetically modified organisms (GMOs). The company's Organic Creamy Ranch Dressing & Dip doesn't have any fillers either; plus it's gluten- and dairy-free, as well as certified USDA organic.

The sauce uses cage-free eggs in the base, alongside organic high oleic sunflower oil, lemon juice, and mustard. This results in a thick, luscious mix that's flavored by various spices and herbs, with tanginess from distilled vinegar. The plant-based dressing is suitable for those following a keto or vegetarian lifestyle. And even though this version is different from the original 1950s ranch recipe, it's still great for marinating fried chicken, serving as a dip for pizza, or simply pouring on salad greens.

Walden Farms is so dedicated to customer satisfaction that the company changed the way it makes its dressings. After hearing people ask for cleaner ingredients, it reformulated the recipes it uses for products like the Ranch Dressing. The dip is now made with olive oil and no artificial flavors. It's also gluten-free and low-calorie, so it can appeal to a wider audience.

The ranch is low-carb, too, with only 1 gram per serving. Being plant-based, it's suitable for vegetarian lifestyles, and it's still made with no sugars, so it's friendly for diabetic people, as well. There are 30 calories per serving, and the olive oil base ensures this dressing only has three grams of total fat in each portion. If you're interested in trying Walden Farms ranch, you can use it in your next batch of mac and cheese along with corn kernels for some nice pops of sweetness.

Drew's Organics doesn't use GMO ingredients or any artificial flavors or colors in any of its dressings. That includes the Creamy Ranch Dressing & Quick Marinade, which is made without artificial preservatives, added sugars, high-fructose corn syrup, or trans fats. The ranch dressing also works as a great marinade for a juicy pork roast or chicken, thanks to its combination of fat, sodium, and vinegars. In fact, reviewers have noted the ranch has a wonderfully oniony taste, with a thick enough texture to stick to a salad or side of fries.

It's also made with organic high oleic sunflower oil, which is a heart-healthy alternative to heavier fats, thanks to being high in monounsaturated fatty acids. These MUFAs are associated with lowering insulin resistance, inflammation, and cardiovascular diseases, according to research published in the Annals of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism. If this is your first time encountering it, high-oleic oil acts like extra virgin olive oil when cooking because the two have very similar fat amounts and types.

Toby's Family Foods has been around since 1978. The company specializes in making each of its eight dressings in batches small enough that every one of them can still be made by hand. There are regular sauces, as well as probiotic ones, including a ranch made with yogurt as a base. Toby's regular Ranch Dressing & Dip is made with clean ingredients, such as buttermilk from cows that aren't given rBST, a synthetic growth hormone that's been linked to certain forms of cancer.

The ranch doesn't use artificial flavors, preservatives, MSG, or synthetic stabilizers, so it has a shorter refrigeration window after opening. Instead of one to two months, Toby's recommends the sauce be finished within two weeks. It also uses non-GMO canola oil that's obtained through high-pressure processing to keep as many of the vitamins and flavor intact as possible. That oil can sometimes separate from the dairy in the ranch, but all you have to do to recombine it is shake or stir the bottle's contents a bit.

Briannas has a long line of dressings and sauces made with high-quality ingredients. The brand's Traditional Ranch is a newer product that, while similar to its Classic Buttermilk Ranch, has fewer calories per serving. This option is also gluten-free, vegetarian, and Kosher Certified.

It's made without high-fructose corn syrup, which many companies use as a cheaper alternative to natural sugars. However, large amounts of high-fructose corn syrup have been linked to liver inflammation, making it something you might want to steer clear of in general. Made in Brenham, Texas, Briannas ranch doesn't have trans fats and is manufactured in a facility without the potential for cross-contamination from nuts.

The company has such a dedication to sustainability that each part of the ranch's (or any other dressing's) bottle can be recycled. That includes the label and cap liner. And to be sure the products meet the brand's high-quality standards, the facility is certified by the SQF, or Safe Quality Food, Institute, which evaluates a business according to strict food manufacturing requirements.

Those who follow vegetarian or vegan lifestyles can be assured there's a ranch for them here, too. Follow Your Heart has been focused on creating intentionally wholesome foods since 1970, which is why the company's Vegan Ranch Dressing is Certified Plant-Based and made without GMO ingredients. It's also gluten-free, thanks to ingredients like xanthan gum, which takes over for gluten in helping the product bind and thicken while keeping it stabilized. The ranch is low in sodium, too, so those watching their salt intake can still enjoy the dressing.

The sauce is reported by fans to be a thick, creamy, and highly versatile addition to a snack or meal. One person even claimed that they could eat the dip by itself. An Amazon reviewer said, "This vegan version of Ranch dressing is stupendous and I am re-ordering it. I cannot add enough superlatives to describe just how good it is."

Marzetti's second entry is from its Simply Dressed line, which was launched in March 2026. Coming from a company that's well over a century old, it's not surprising these new products have already gotten good reviews for taste and consistency.

Sauces in this line, like the Homestyle Ranch Dressing & Dip, are made with both canola and extra virgin olive oils. This means it has no trans fats, which is better for customers' long-term heart health. The dressing is also safe for those leading vegetarian lifestyles.

Like the classic ranch, it's made without high fructose corn syrup, preservatives, and artificial colors or flavors. But the Simply Dressed version has fewer calories per serving and is gluten-free. Shoppers can use the sauce as a dip on its own, or it can be combined with a bit of sour cream or a soft cheese to make it thicker and add even more creamy texture.

Determining the ranch dressing brands with the cleanest ingredients was an interesting task to tackle. We first searched for clean-ingredient and organic brands that made ranch dressing before making a list of the dips and sauces that met our high standards. The dressings had to be made without artificial ingredients, minimally processed, and free of synthetic preservatives to make it onto the final list presented here.

#9548. Not Regular Butter Or Mayo: Use This Spread To Give Breakfast Burritos A Delicious, Crunchy Exterior

Breakfast burritos originated in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and have now become a popular way to start the day across the U.S. — they are even available at McDonald's! The typical combination of eggs, meats, and cheese wrapped in a tortilla is not only packed with flavor and protein but is also a conveniently portable food.

There are many variations on a breakfast burrito recipe, such as changing up the type of cheese or switching up the meats, but these ignore what holds it all together: the tortilla. You can just wrap your fillings in one and call it a day, but you know that it's much better (and crunchier) when you toast it, and you need a little fat to get the job done. Butter is a great solution, but using garlic butter will impart so much additional flavor to your finished breakfast burrito.

Garlic butter isn't some type of fat made from garlic, though. Instead, it's part of a larger category of foods called compound butters, which consist of regular dairy butter blended with a variety of seasonings and other ingredients to add flavor. Since many herbs and spices contain fat-soluble flavor compounds, the butter becomes infused with the aromas of whatever is added to it, including garlic. So, when you toast your breakfast burrito in garlic butter, the fat itself has a garlicky kick that will get transferred to your tortilla. It will also save you the hassle of frying garlic in butter to get a similar effect.

To make your breakfast burrito extra crispy with garlic butter, you simply need to wrap your burrito in a flour tortilla, which is the most flexible for making this breakfast favorite and tends to come in larger sizes compared to corn tortillas. You can assemble several burritos this way if you want to meal prep. Then, melt about a tablespoon of garlic butter in a pan over medium heat and place your burrito in the pan seam-side down to seal it. Turn it over to toast the other side, and promptly remove it from the pan. For more even browning, you can place a flat tortilla in the pan, add all your fillings, and then remove it to roll up, making sure to tuck in the sides. You can also grease a muffin tin with garlic butter to make breakfast burrito bites.

There are many commercially available garlic butters you can find at supermarkets, including one made by Kerrygold, but they can often be more expensive per ounce than regular butter, even from premium brands. Fortunately, compound butters — including variations on plain garlic butter — are very easy to make at home. David Guas' roasted garlic compound butter, for example, can be frozen for up to three months and is customizable. You can add finely minced herbs, like parsley and thyme. If you don't have fresh herbs, you can also use dried versions, though give your compound butter some extra time for the flavors to marry.

#9546. 11 Common Mistakes Everyone Makes When Peeling Fruit

There's lots of chatter online about the best ways to peel all kinds of fruit, and the debate may just rage on forever. Regardless of how you feel about the many creative methods that seem to gain so much attention, there are a few mistakes you would be wise to avoid. Why? Well, when you sidestep these common blunders, you not only cut down on unnecessary waste, but also create less of a mess along the way and speed up the process as a whole. Sounds like a win-win-win to us.

From peeling your bananas in the wrong direction to trying to peel tomatoes without blanching them first to not utilizing a spoon to help you scoop avocado meat from the skin, many of the missteps found below are ones plenty of people commit every day. So, even if you think you already know the best way to peel a particular type of fruit, you may be surprised to learn there's a more efficient or tidy way to get the job done. Are you already in the know, or are you falling prey to frequent mistakes unbeknownst to you? Let's find out.

You'd be hard-pressed to find someone who hasn't tried to peel an orange using nothing but their hands before. However, doing so is the first fruit-peeling mistake on our list. If you've ever done it that way and found yourself attempting to remove the white, stringy pith to no avail, you already know why, too. Thankfully, though, there's a way to avoid this and cut down on the bothersome, bitter-tasting membranes, and it isn't complicated. All you need to do is employ a little help from a knife. Not only will it get the job done quickly and correctly, but it'll also save you from having to scrape remnants of the orange peel from under your fingernails as well — and most of us are all too familiar with how annoying that can be.

To peel an orange while avoiding the majority of the pith (aka the right way), start by setting it on a cutting board stem side up. Then, use an extra-sharp knife to make a vertical cut just off the side of the stem, straight down to the bottom. Continue doing this four times in total, in a box shape, so you are left with a rectangular center piece. The middle section will contain most of the pith, so feel free to toss it out. After that, you can simply enjoy the four orange wedges straight from the peel. It's that easy.

A major complaint people have about peaches is that they don't enjoy consuming the fuzzy skin very much. As a result, knowing how to peel them will serve you well. Even so, many people don't even think about removing the skin, or they reach for a peeling tool, and unfortunately, that's a mistake with the gentle fruit. While handy, the kitchen tool is much too abrasive for the tender skin and meat of a peach, so they rip right through them and often leave you with a juicy mess and significantly less fruit to enjoy. Nobody wants that. Luckily, there's a better way. You just need to blanch and shock the peaches quickly, and the skins will basically slide right off.

To utilize the blanch and shock method, start by cutting a small X pattern into the bottom of whole peaches. Then, lower them into a pot of boiling water with a slotted spoon. Leave the peaches in the boiling water for about 1 to 3 minutes, depending on how ripe they are — the riper they are, the less time they'll need, but you'll know they are done when the scored sections start to peel back. After that, remove the peaches and submerge them in an ice bath to quickly cool them off and prevent them from cooking. After about five minutes, extract the peaches and use your hands to quickly and easily peel back the skins, starting from the scored section.

Mangoes are a stone (or drupe) fruit. As such, they contain a large pit in the center, and this can make peeling them complicated, especially since the flesh is so tender. However, you can easily manage the task if you utilize the best method for peeling mangoes, which involves scoring a grid pattern in the outer portions of the mango after the core is removed. When you do, you are left with simple-to-remove cubes of fruit that are perfect for munching solo or incorporating into recipes of all kinds.

To start, set a mango on a cutting board and hold it upright with the stem at the top. The next step is to use a sharp knife to make vertical cuts from the top to bottom on all four sides about ¼ inch from the center. This removes the pit and leaves you with four sides containing all the good stuff. After that, use your knife to score a grid pattern in each portion, taking care not to cut through the skin itself. When this is done, push up from the skin side so you wind up with rows of protruding cubes of fruit. All that's left for you to do at this point is to use a spoon to scoop them out. Your knife will work as a scoop as well, but the room for error increases, as it can easily cut through the skin. So, if you want to play it safe, spoon it is.

Peeling tomatoes seems like a challenging task, but it must be done if you want to turn them into a basic sauce or can them. The skins are relatively tough, and the fruit beneath is tender enough to fall apart with minimal pressure from a knife or peeling tool. Don't even get us started on how easily the juice squeezes out, either. In fact, the process is daunting enough that many people simply reach for canned tomatoes to avoid the mess and effort, which can feel futile if you don't do it the right way. Speaking of which, the best, easiest way to peel tomatoes starts with blanching them, so don't make the mistake of attempting to get the job done without doing so.

Blanching tomatoes may sound fancy to some, but it couldn't be simpler. To start. Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. While you wait, score small X patterns into the bottom of the tomatoes you wish to peel. When the water is ready, drop them in and leave them for about 30 to 40 seconds; anything longer than that and you run the risk of the fruit becoming too mushy to handle. Then, extract them from the water with a slotted spoon and put them directly into an ice bath. After about two to three minutes, you can start pulling them out and using your hands to quickly and easily slide the tomato skins off.

You don't have to peel apples to enjoy them — the skins are edible, after all. Still, if you want to hone in on the tart, sweet fruit below without the peels getting in the way, or add them to a recipe that calls for skinned ones, removing them is always an option. However, there are many methods people employ, some of which are much more effective than others. With this in mind, choosing not to utilize what has been deemed the donut ring method is a mistake. It is quick, easy, and helps minimize waste as well. Since that's the goal, you're going to want to commit it to memory.

Whether you prefer to use a paring knife or a vegetable peeler, the donut ring method is the way to go when it comes to peeling apples. Regardless of your preferred tool, start by cutting a ring around the top and bottom of your apple. Then, use your knife or peeler to slice vertically from top to bottom, connecting the two initial circles.

Once you are all done, you don't have to toss the stem and skin into the trash, either. Instead, you can completely eliminate waste by making a Peel-To-Stem Apple Pie. We know this sounds counterintuitive since we spend so much time removing them in the first place, but don't knock it until you try it.

Pear skins are edible, but there are plenty of times when peeling them is in order, such as when you are making a pie or canning them. The skins aren't very tough, either, so using a vegetable peeler isn't off the table. However, if you need to peel more than one, there's a much easier way to achieve your goal: Blanching and shocking them. This isn't the first time we've said this about peeling fruit, but with pears, it truly is a game-changer that allows the skins to simply slide right off with the brush of your fingers. So, choosing not to use the method when peeling batches of pears would be a time-consuming blunder you don't want to commit.

To properly blanch pears, submerge them in a pot of water that is boiling or just under. As long as the water is piping hot, it'll work its skin-peeling magic. Leave the fruit in the pot for about 10 seconds, maybe 15 at most. Then, remove one and drop it into a bowl of ice-cold water. Before removing the rest of the pears from the pot, check them to make sure you left the extracted one in the hot water long enough by rubbing the skin. If it comes off easily, transfer the remaining pears to the ice bath. If not, pop the initial pear back in the hot water for a few more seconds before removing them all.

Pineapple is arguably the best tropical fruit of them all, but even if you don't feel that way, it is a tricky fruit to peel. The outer layer of eyes is extremely dense and hard, so it's not like a vegetable peeler will do the trick. A sharp knife is undoubtedly a must. However, where you begin the cutting process matters, and not starting by creating a flat base is not the way to go. If you skip ahead of the step, the pineapple's curved bottom makes slicing precarious and unstable at best.

Thankfully, creating a stable base on a pineapple is easy-peasy, and then the rest of the peeling process effortlessly falls into place. Simply lay the fruit on its side and grip the top while slicing through the base to create a flat end piece. Then, do the same on the top and stand the entire fruit upright. From there, cut the hard core out by slicing from the top to bottom on all four sides, leaving a small rectangular cube in the center. After that, you can slice the fleshy parts of the pineapple into cubes, long slices, or however you like.

Papayas have a distinct musky flavor backed up by lots of sweetness. While some say it is an acquired taste, there's almost nothing that compares once you develop it. Even so, it contains lots of small black seeds, which, while edible, bring a strong, mustardy, peppery, bitter element to the table that most people don't want to munch along with the fruit itself. With this in mind, knowing how to peel a papaya properly is essential. The first mistake people often commit is trying to skin a papaya whole. It may be easy to do, but once the fruit is peeled, it becomes slippery, making it challenging to handle and remove the seeds. That's why it is important to cut the ends off and halve it first.

After halving a whole papaya, the seeds inside are fully exposed, allowing you to easily scoop them out with nothing more than a spoon. Whether you save them to add to another dish or not is up to you, but if it's the sweet, fleshy fruit you are after, the job is nearly done at this point. All that's left is to slide a paring knife just above the skin to separate it from the fruit. Then, you can slice or chop it however you like.

Pomegranates are nutrient-dense and rich in antioxidants, making them a healthy fruit to enjoy. They also boast a deliciously unique sweet, tangy, tart flavor profile that many love. Unfortunately, though, getting to the tasty edible seeds within the fruit isn't as simple as you might hope. Pomegranates contain loads of pith, the seeds don't separate super easily, and the potent red fruit stains like no other, so if you happen to break open a few seeds along the way, your hands or clothes could show the signs of it for quite some time. Thankfully, there is a quick fix for all of these issues: Peeling them underwater. When you do, the colorful juice dilutes before it gets a chance to stain, the pith floats to the top, and the seeds come apart significantly easier. The underwater method also reduces waste, making it the absolute best way to go.

There isn't any fancy trick to using the underwater method for peeling pomegranates. Simply crack open the fruit and submerge it in a bowl of water. Using your hands, start to break apart the seeds and watch as the pith and outer peel float to the top. When all of the seeds are separated, use a slotted spoon to remove the floating waste. Finish off by extracting the seeds and placing them on a paper towel or clean cloth to dry.

Avocados feature a whole slew of health benefits, such as being high in fiber, nutrients, and healthy fats. They are even widely considered a superfood, so knowing how to tap into their potential, i.e., being able to peel them like a pro, is something everyone should know how to do. Regardless, the tough outer shell and large, hard seed in the middle of the avocado mean there are some good and bad ways to peel them. Not using a spoon to help you manage the task is one such mistake you don't want to commit because, plain and simple, it makes the job more complicated than it needs to be.

The best way to peel an avocado starts by slicing into the fruit lengthwise around the seed until you create a complete ring. Then, holding one hand on either side, gently twist, and the two halves should come apart easily, at least if it is ripe. Next, smack your knife into the seed with enough force that it sticks. Twist the knife, and the seed should come right out. Now the two halves are ready for you to slice or cube as desired. Choose your shape and use your knife to create either strips or a grid pattern, taking care not to puncture the skin below. Then, you can easily use a spoon to scoop out the avocado chunks and enjoy.

Interestingly, the way people peel a banana is somewhat of a controversial topic. Do you start at the stem at the top or the nub at the bottom? Many people simply grab a banana and start peeling from the stem without even thinking about it. However, plenty of others claim that is the wrong way, and instead, reach for the bottom nub and hold the stem like a handle — just like monkeys do. While the debate may never end on Reddit and other online forums, we are fans of the "monkey method."

When you use the stem as a handle, you can grip a banana much more firmly without worrying about potentially bruising the delicate fruit inside the peel — something that happens more easily than you might think. In addition, all it takes to split open the skin near the bottom nub is a gentle pinch. Then, you can simply peel back small strips and start munching or dicing as you please. When you go about it the opposite way — what many think is backwards — it takes more force to split the stem from the skin, and it's much easier to smush some of the fruit inside. No, thanks. Neither way may be 100% wrong, but give the monkey method a try and something tells us you'll never look back again. Besides, who can argue with a cute little built-in handle?

#9543. Skip The Oven: This Easy Turkey Dinner Is Ready In Half The Time

With Thanksgiving just around the corner, many of us are gearing up to spend time with friends and family, and enjoy a delicious meal. For those who are hosting and doing the cooking, however, there is considerably more to the holiday. Aside from cleaning the house top to bottom, preparing a huge meal, including a whole turkey, can be stressful to say the least. Eschewing the turkey might take a major burden off your plate, but if you don't want to go fully historical with your Thanksgiving feast (the Plymouth settlers likely ate different game birds and venison) you might instead opt for oven-free, skillet-cooked turkey meatballs in a savory gravy.

Meatballs are an excellent option because you can stuff the flavors of Thanksgiving turkey and stuffing into them, minus the hours of cook time. In fact, if you consider a 20 pound turkey takes four to five hours to roast, and making turkey meatballs takes an hour, tops (depending on how long it takes you to roll them all out), you're saving yourself a lot of time. It also means your oven is completely free for all the delicious sides, like hopefully mistake-free green bean casserole and hot, pillowy rolls. Further, this is a great meal to pull out any time of the year when you want a Thanksgiving turkey-like dinner, without the fuss.

If you're looking for inspiration on what ingredients to use in your turkey meatballs, we have some suggestions (and it's worth noting that none of these ideas add any significant time to the meatball preparation). It's not the best idea to use straight ground turkey because it tends to be quite lean; as you can see in the video above, the creator also includes Italian sausage, which has much-needed fat to help keep the balls moist and tender. If you don't want to use sausage, though, you could take Ina Garten's advice and use prosciutto, or see if you can find ground turkey thighs, as opposed to breast meat, because it has a higher fat content.

Of course to get that real Thanksgiving dinner taste, you'll also want to use plenty of herbs. Sage has a savory, meaty flavor that will boldly season those meatballs, while thyme adds warmth and earthiness; both are often used in stuffing, and they'll pair nicely with your ground turkey and sausage as well. A little rosemary brings a peppery, piney flavor into the mix, and parsley brightens with its herbaceousness.

For a sweet spin that adds another element of a popular Thanksgiving dish, toss in some dried cranberries that have been diced into little bits as well, or try pomegranate-infused Craisins. A touch of citrus zest, too, incorporates some sweetness and complexity.

#9540. When Scientists Admit Mistakes, That Means Science Is Working

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When the first cases of COVID-19 were discovered in a hospital in Wuhan, I had already studied the U.S. public health response to seven epidemics and pandemics. I am no stranger to the role of politics in pandemic response. Still, the recent Senate hearings grilling Dr. Anthony Fauci alarmed me.

Fauci is a physician and immunologist who served as the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and as chief medical advisor to President Trump during the period of Covid-19—who has subsequently become a scapegoat for those who didn’t like the restrictions that came with the pandemic. As Senator Rand Paul put it, based on the evidence-free conspiracy theory that Dr. Fauci funded research that led to the pandemic: “One million Americans died from COVID and not even an apology from Dr. Anthony Fauci.”

While we might recognize such claims as preposterous, it would be a mistake to treat these hearings as mere political theater. Those who are treating errors in the understanding of Covid-19 as criminal threaten one of the most important public goods we have during an infectious disease crisis: the willingness of experts to publicly admit mistakes.

Dr. Fauci has openly acknowledged missteps, communication errors, and evolving judgments in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic—an honesty that is not matched by his critics. Instead, his honesty has been leveraged by them to sow doubt in science itself.

But the reason we turn to experts during a crisis is not because they are omniscient. Of course they aren’t. It is because they learn faster and better than non-experts. Learning, however, is a naturally error-prone process. And learning when a novel infectious disease is fueling a global pandemic is particularly so. One can hope that scientists responding to such a crisis will be able to reduce uncertainties in a linear and predictable fashion. But that is not the norm.

As a social scientist, if I discover something new, when I present my findings to my colleagues, the most likely result is that they will tell me all the ways they think I might be wrong. My job is to prove that my findings hold even after considering their counterarguments. Skepticism is essential in the process of separating fact from fiction. We have more confidence in results that have survived such pressure-testing.

Experts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) during the pandemic received just this type of skepticism from other experts. And yet much of the political commentary surrounding these normal and essential controversies cited the evidence of controversy as proof the CDC was flailing.

This approach treats science as though the discovery of new facts unfolds like a treasure hunt where the first person to find the treasure opens the lid and everyone can see the treasure with their own eyes. In a treasure hunt, discovery and validation are essentially the same thing.

But science does not work this way. Take the discovery of HIV. Dr. Luc Montaignier identified the virus under an electron microscope in February 1983. Uncertainty surrounding whether the virus was causative or opportunistic led to more than a year of additional research, culminating in four papers published by Dr. Robert Gallo and his colleagues in 1984, that affirmed Montaignier’s finding. According to Montaignier, it was one of these publications, in particular, that “convinced the scientific community that this new retrolentivirus was the cause of AIDS.”

This example shows something that is true across the sciences. New discoveries that eventually become accepted as scientific facts can linger for an extended period as mere “claims” while uncertainties are addressed.

Critics argue that the scientific uncertainty around the discovery of the AIDS virus was unnecessarily prolonged and cost lives. If moving quickly on yet-to-be-validated evidence is the right approach during a pandemic, note that Fauci and his public health colleagues are currently being attacked for doing exactly that. Public health experts believed at the outset that COVID-19 was like SARS, with transmission most likely to occur late in the course of infection. Hence the guidance that directed the public and health care workers to wear masks when caring for patients already showing symptoms. Mounting evidence of asymptomatic infection eventually proved that COVID-19 transmission was very different from SARS, leading to new masking guidance.

When should public health experts act on early, but unvalidated, evidence versus taking the time to iron out uncertainties? While it may look obvious in hindsight, there is no magic formula that can sort out in advance when the better course will have been to slow down and validate versus act on plausible, but still uncertain, claims.

Climate scientists would almost certainly never argue their experience in the public eye has been a picnic. But they had one big advantage over those trying to guide the response to a pandemic driven by a novel infectious disease. Climate scientists had decades—as opposed to only weeks or days—to conduct research before they were asked to explain what they knew to the public. In fact, climate scientists did not always expect warming to result from burning fossil fuels. Up until the 1950s, the prevailing wisdom was that the oceans would absorb excess carbon dioxide so that there would be minimal if any warming. Roger Revelle and Hans Seuss, who together discovered the error, both received awards for their research.

When a novel infectious disease comes to town, the first cases detected are rarely the actual start of the outbreak. There are no tests to make a positive diagnosis. Some of the suspected cases turn out to have other causes. People who are infected are overlooked. Data collected at the outset is patchy and error-prone. As the public health community pivots to emergency response footing, they begin to collect data more systematically. Even so, new data can rapidly overturn early assumptions. The case definition for COVID-19 was updated almost weekly during the first 10 weeks of the pandemic.

Monday morning quarterbacking is easy. Try advising countries on how to manage a growing pandemic while the ground is moving beneath your feet.

As the United States’ performance during the COVID-19 pandemic is reviewed, even those who are not engaging in political grandstanding tend to reduce the effort to a scorecard that tallies the times experts were right versus the times they were wrong. Even if the reversals are few in number, they are barely tolerated. We usually give examinations to people after they have had time to learn and master the material. What is the right metric to use for public health experts who are trying to inform us when the answers are still being discovered?

Speaking of treasure, I think we were lucky during COVID-19 to have public health experts who were willing to admit mistakes as soon as they were discovered. Things will go markedly worse for us if, during the next pandemic, they are less forthcoming.

An earlier version of this article first appeared on MS NOW.

Ann Keller, Ph.D., is an associate professor of health politics & policy at UC Berkeley School of Public Health.

#9539. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9538. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9537. Give Grilled Cheese A Major Flavor And Protein Boost With One Hearty Addition

There are seemingly as many kinds of grilled cheese as there are individuals on this planet. There are, for example, plenty of international styles worth trying, while even the classic all-American versions can consist of a variety of cheeses, like American, cheddar, Gouda, and Havarti. You might like to make yours using mayonnaise on the bread, while your neighbor prefers butter in the pan. And then there are extra fillings and additions. Some people add a little bacon and maple syrup to their sandwiches, while others turn theirs into a breakfast masterpiece with an egg. Another fantastically tasty option is to add chili, which not only imbues the meal with a huge dose of extra flavor, but also gives you a nice protein boost.

Whether you have more leftover chili than you know what to do with, or a can or two in your pantry collecting dust, it's actually the perfect addition. It's savory, hearty, and saucy, which works so well when layered with cheese (which chili often gets topped with) and sandwiched between two slices of bread, pan-browned to crispy perfection. And if you have daily protein goals, a ¼ cup of chili, which is a reasonable starting quantity for a single sandwich, can typically get you roughly 4 to 5 grams closer to meeting that target (though this will vary depending on the recipe).

One of the best things about chili grilled cheese sandwiches is how easy they are to make. You can assemble them in the pan like normal, but add a scoop of chili onto one slice of bread before closing it up. This works well if you're just making one or two sandwiches, but if you have more mouths to feed, you can actually make a whole bunch in the oven at once. You'll just want to be sure to spread butter on the outside of each slice of bread, combine your chili with plenty of shredded cheese to make a gooey, melty filling, and then flip the sandwiches halfway through baking so both sides get nice and toasty.

Now, like all grilled cheeses, this variation is still quite customizable. For example, if you wanted to add some sharpness to help cut through all the richness of the other ingredients, you could sprinkle green onion on top of the chili. Alternatively, if you wanted a bite, plus a bit of spice, sliced or chopped jalapeños would do nicely (or you might make the sweet pickled version known as cowboy candy). To amp up the protein even more, some bacon wouldn't be out of place, either. You could also lean into the idea of a chili cheese dog grilled cheese, and slice a hot dog lengthwise, fry it up, and place that on top of the chili layer.
